personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Harry's dominant traits in OotP are simmering, volcanic anger; a fierce need for information he's been denied; impulsive protectiveness; pride wounded by exclusion; deep moral seriousness about truth-telling; and emotional volatility that he is frequently ashamed of but cannot control. His voice is direct, often cutting, and his internal monologue reveals layers of self-doubt beneath the bravado. He uses sarcasm as a weapon ('I'm terrified now'), makes self-aware observations about his own faults (the prefect badge sequence shows genuine self-examination), and alternates between explosive outbursts and cold calm. He interrogates his own motivations honestly — the passage where he examines whether he expected the prefect badge, and whether that makes him arrogant, is a key example. His anger is rendered in capital letters, obsessive repetition, and physical symptoms (searing scar, trembling hands). His voice also carries dry humour ('You're not going to be able to bank on more than five minutes'), genuine warmth toward his friends, and a deep stubbornness about truth ('I'm not lying and I'm not mad').
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves Harry's anger and defiance fairly well: he shouts at Umbridge in class ('It was murder. Voldemort killed him'), confronts Malfoy without flinching, snaps at Ron ('I said I'm fine, Ron!'), and delivers the key line about Voldemort in the Atrium ('You're the weak one, and you'll never know love, or friendship'). His protectiveness of Sirius drives the entire second half of the film. His sarcasm appears occasionally ('I must not tell lies' to Umbridge after the centaurs take her). However, large swathes of his interior voice are absent. The film never shows his self-examination, his shame about his anger, or his capacity for nuanced moral reflection. The prefect-badge internal monologue is entirely gone. His obsessive monitoring of the news, his frustrated theorising, his guilt about Cedric, his complex feelings about his father after the Pensieve — all absent or severely truncated. The film Harry is angrier and simpler than the book Harry. His voice is preserved in broad strokes but the granularity — the hesitation, the self-correction, the dark humour — is mostly gone.
personality_voice.difference: The book Harry is complex and self-interrogating beneath his rage; the film Harry is predominantly reactive-angry. Key speech patterns — the dry sarcasm, the honest self-doubt, the obsessive internal arguments — are absent or heavily reduced. The film captures his defiance and protectiveness but loses the texture of his voice.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: This is a meaningful compression that removes secondary traits (self-examination, dry humour, emotional granularity) while preserving the dominant one (anger/defiance). The character is recognisable but notably simplified. Score sits in the 18–22 range rather than higher because the simplification is substantial — a whole register of Harry's personality (the honest, reflective, self-critical voice) is lost.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Harry is the central protagonist and driving agent throughout OotP. He initiates the DA, he challenges Umbridge directly and repeatedly, he investigates Voldemort's plans through his scar-visions, he pushes for information from adults (Sirius, the Order), he reaches the conclusion about the Department of Mysteries independently, and he leads the expedition there. He also makes the key decision to check on Sirius via Umbridge's fire, even against Hermione's advice. In terms of plot decisions, nearly every major turning point passes through Harry's choice: forming the DA, going to the Ministry, not surrendering the prophecy. His agency is maximally high.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves Harry's central agency well: he initiates or co-initiates the DA (though Hermione's role is slightly expanded — she explicitly corrects herself after saying it was Harry's idea, suggesting she's covering for him, which preserves the ambiguity), he leads the Ministry expedition, he makes the final call to go even against Hermione's warnings, and he confronts Voldemort in the Atrium. His agency in the Umbridge confrontation is fully preserved — he refuses to back down, insists on truth-telling, and deliberately defies authority. The key moments where Harry drives the plot are all present.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Minor agency reductions: the film compresses Harry's independent theorising about Voldemort's weapon; some exposition is delivered to him by other characters rather than worked out by him. The DA organisation montage reduces his teaching role slightly. But no major agency is transferred away from him. The Pensieve scene is present but truncated, and the decision to sneak into Snape's Pensieve is preserved.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Harry retains his central role and the decisive acts of agency. Small reductions in his investigative and teaching agency are present but do not constitute a major transfer. Score in the 14–17 range, close to the top, because the compression is real but not damaging.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Harry's motivations in OotP are layered: he wants to be trusted and included by the Order and by Dumbledore, he wants to fight Voldemort directly rather than be kept passive, he is driven by guilt and grief over Cedric, he is terrified of expulsion and losing his place in the wizarding world, and he is increasingly anxious that the connection to Voldemort may be corrupting him. His internal conflict between trusting Dumbledore and resenting his exclusion is central. The 'saving-people thing' Hermione identifies is both a strength and a vulnerability he cannot fully acknowledge. His fear that he is 'becoming bad' because of the Voldemort connection is explicitly articulated and deeply felt.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the primary motivations clearly: Harry's need to fight, his protective drive toward Sirius ('he's the only family I've got left'), his defiance of Umbridge's suppression of truth. The 'saving-people thing' accusation by Hermione is present in the film. The fear that he might be 'becoming bad' is explicitly stated in a conversation with Sirius at Grimmauld Place ('What if I'm becoming more like him?'). His anger at exclusion is present. However, the deeper layer — his guilt over Cedric, his terror of expulsion, his complex resentment of Dumbledore specifically — is largely reduced to generic frustration. The internal conflict about his father (post-Pensieve) is severely compressed; the Pensieve scene is present but the aftermath — Harry's shattering of the comfortable image of James Potter and what it does to his sense of identity — is entirely absent from the theatrical cut.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: Primary motivations (fight Voldemort, protect Sirius, assert truth) are preserved. Secondary motivations (guilt about Cedric, terror of expulsion, identity crisis about father) are mostly absent. The conflict about Dumbledore withholding information is simplified to generic exclusion rather than the specific, personalised resentment of the books.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but not fundamentally wrong. The core is intact; the secondary layers are missing. Score in the 11–13 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Harry's arc in OotP is one of the most complex in the series: he begins isolated, furious, and excluded; he builds agency and community through the DA; he is seduced by his connection to Voldemort into a catastrophic error of judgment; he loses Sirius as a direct consequence; he receives the full weight of the prophecy; and he ends the book not triumphant but sobered — understanding his destiny, his isolation, and his responsibility in a new way. Crucially, the arc includes his disillusionment with his father (Pensieve), his recognition of his own 'saving-people' flaw, and his final conversation with Dumbledore in which he smashes the office before being told the truth. The ending is not a victory but a reckoning.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves the broad shape of the arc: isolation, DA-building, Ministry disaster, Sirius's death, Voldemort confrontation. The DA portion is well-handled and shows Harry growing in agency and leadership. The Ministry sequence and Sirius's death are faithful. However, the post-Sirius arc — Harry's rage at Dumbledore, the office destruction, the full prophecy revelation — is present in the theatrical cut but only in compressed form. The 'Dumbledore and Harry in the office' scene is listed as a cut scene, which means the extended reckoning (Harry smashing instruments, Dumbledore's apology, the full explanation of why Harry was kept in the dark) is absent from the theatrical release. What remains is a shortened exchange. The Pensieve aftermath, which is a crucial arc step, is absent. Harry ends the film with a hopeful, forward-looking speech ('something worth fighting for') that softens the book's far more ambiguous, grief-stricken ending.
character_arc.difference: The arc's turning points are present but several key steps are missing or compressed: the full Pensieve aftermath (identity crisis about James), the office destruction scene (the emotional culmination of the exclusion arc), and the final grief-reckoning. The ending is tonally different — the book ends in grief and hard-won understanding; the film ends with qualified hope.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is incomplete. The film rushes through the post-Sirius reckoning, skips the office destruction entirely (a crucial cathartic step in the arc), and converts the ending from grief to hope. These are important steps in Harry's arc, not minor details. Score in the 8–10 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Harry's most important relationships in OotP are: (1) Sirius — Harry's primary emotional anchor, source of warmth and risk; (2) Dumbledore — a relationship defined by painful distance, withheld information, and Harry's resentment; (3) Ron and Hermione — Harry's outbursts and their patient loyalty tested; (4) Snape — mutual loathing, Occlumency lessons, Pensieve violation; (5) Cho — awkward romantic pursuit intertwined with Cedric's death; (6) Luna — unexpected emotional resonance. Each relationship has distinct texture.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: Sirius relationship: well-preserved. The warmth, the risk-taking, the paternal dynamic are all present. The Grimmauld Place reunion and conversation about Harry 'becoming bad' are faithful. His death and Harry's grief are handled effectively. Dumbledore relationship: the physical avoidance is present (Dumbledore notably does not look at Harry throughout the film) and the post-Department-of-Mysteries conversation preserves the emotional core ('I care too much about you'), though it is compressed. The full reckoning of the book is absent. Ron/Hermione: Harry's anger at them for keeping information is present but the depth of his alienation and reconciliation is reduced. Snape: the Occlumency relationship and Pensieve violation are present but the aftermath — Harry's understanding that Snape was genuinely trying to help him, and the complexity of Snape's past — is truncated. Cho: the relationship's messiness (the crying, the Cedric connection, the misunderstanding) is present in outline. Luna: the thestral scene and the grief-bonding conversation are preserved and emotionally faithful.
key_relationships.difference: The Dumbledore relationship loses its most important dynamic: Harry's personalised resentment and the full explanation of why he was excluded. The Snape relationship loses most of its complexity after the Pensieve. The Ron/Hermione bonds are present but their emotional texture (Harry's genuine alienation and reconciliation) is reduced.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Key relationships are mostly faithful in broad strokes but several important dynamics are weakened. The Dumbledore relationship particularly loses its specific, personalised texture. Score in the 7–8 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: OotP is the book in which Harry is most morally and psychologically complex. He is flawed in specific, observable ways: he rants at his friends without justification, he fails at Occlumency because he refuses to face his own emotions, he makes a catastrophic error of judgment that leads directly to Sirius's death, he has a humbling encounter with his father's ugliness in the Pensieve, and he spends much of the book in a state of narcissistic isolation that he only partially escapes. He is also shown at his best: teaching the DA with genuine skill and care, showing unexpected empathy (Luna's missing shoes, Neville's parents at St Mungo's), and maintaining dignity in situations that would break others (Umbridge's quill). The prefect badge sequence shows him at his most honest and self-aware. His obsessive news-watching, his guilt about Cedric, his complex reaction to the prophecy — all build a portrait of a specific, flawed, real person.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves Harry's capacity for anger, defiance, and leadership. The DA scenes show him as a genuinely good teacher. The 'becoming bad' conversation with Sirius shows some interiority. However, enormous amounts of defining complexity are absent: the prefect-badge self-examination is entirely gone; his obsessive monitoring of the news and guilt about being excluded are reduced to a brief mention; his reaction to the Pensieve (the shattering of his image of his father) is present only in the scene where he exits the Pensieve abruptly, without the extended aftermath; his guilt about Sirius's death — his recognition that the 'saving-people thing' was his flaw and that he caused Sirius's death — is present in compressed form but not the full, agonising reckoning of the book; the Neville's parents scene at St Mungo's is absent; the Luna shoe-grief scene that closes the book is present and well-handled. Several scenes listed as cut (Neville defending Harry, life in Gryffindor Tower, Harry's post-Sirius packing) remove texture that built Harry's daily social existence and emotional state.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film loses: the prefect badge sequence (honest self-examination); the full post-Pensieve identity crisis; the post-Sirius office destruction and reckoning; the St Mungo's scene (Harry's empathy toward Neville); the obsessive news-watching as a character beat; and the full Dumbledore exclusion arc. What remains is recognisable but substantially simplified.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Significant complexity is removed. The character is not reduced to a single trait, but the specific, uncomfortable, morally complex texture of book Harry — his capacity for ugly self-pity alongside genuine heroism, his flaw of 'saving-people' causing real catastrophe, his humbling by his father's ugliness — is largely absent from the film. Score in the 8–10 range.

The obsessive news-monitoring sequences — Harry's frustrated isolation in Privet Drive — largely cut (only brief reference in opening)

score_caps_applied: Cap at 85 considered: film removes major complexity, agency contradiction (post-Pensieve arc, office destruction, prefect sequence) — cap applied
Cap at 80 considered: key relationships (Dumbledore dynamic, Snape aftermath) are altered — contributes to score placement
Final score of 70 reflects: broad faithfulness in personality, agency and motivation preserved in outline, but substantial loss of complexity, nuance, arc steps and key relationship texture
key_observations: The film's Harry Potter is a faithful broad-strokes adaptation that successfully preserves his most visible traits — defiance, protectiveness, anger at institutional dishonesty, leadership in the DA — while losing most of the internal complexity that makes book Harry one of the series' most morally rich portraits. The film captures the character's exterior correctly but misses his interior: the self-examination, the shame about his own anger, the humbling encounter with his father's ugliness, and the full catharsis of his grief after Sirius's death. The theatrical cut's removal of the office-destruction scene is the single most damaging adaptation choice, as it eliminates the emotional climax of Harry's arc — his rage at Dumbledore and the reckoning that follows. The ending's conversion from grief-and-hard-truth to qualified hope further softens a character who, in the book, ends the story sobered and permanently changed rather than reinvigorated. The DA scenes and the Ministry sequence are well-handled and preserve Harry's agency and courage. The relationship with Sirius is the best-preserved key relationship. The score of 70 reflects a character who is recognisably Harry Potter in action and broad motivation, but who has lost the specific, uncomfortable, self-aware complexity that defines him in the source text.
